prompt.context_jp: クライアント先の会議室に、鶸田と鷹野の姿____あった。
prompt.prompt_jp: クライアント先の会議室に、鶸田と鷹野の姿____あった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that fits this opening line.

feedback.correct_en: This is the chapter's opening sentence — the two characters are being introduced as new information in the scene. Existential 「〜がある/いる」 with brand-new referents takes が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would mark them as an already-established topic, which is wrong for a scene-setting first line. を doesn't fit an intransitive existence verb.

contrast_examples.en: There was a cat in the room. (new information)
The cat was by the window. (already-known topic)

prompt.context_jp: プレゼン資料を手にした鶸田____、緊張で声がわずかにうわずっている。
prompt.prompt_jp: プレゼン資料を手にした鶸田____、緊張で声がわずかにうわずっている。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle marking Hiwada here.

feedback.correct_en: Hiwada was introduced in the prior sentence, so he is now the established topic the narrator comments on. は sets him as the frame, and the real new information (「声がわずかにうわずっている」) comes with が inside the clause.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would re-introduce him as new, which contradicts sentence 1. The が/は split within this sentence is itself a model: topic は at the outer level, descriptive が at the inner level.

contrast_examples.jp: 鶸田は声が震えていた。
contrast_examples.en: As for Hiwada, his voice was trembling. (topic + descriptive が)

contrast_examples.jp: 鶸田が声を震わせていた。
contrast_examples.en: It was Hiwada whose voice was trembling. (identificational)

prompt.context_jp: 自分の口から飛び出した苦しまぎれの冗談____、会議室の空気をむしろ重くした。
prompt.prompt_jp: 自分の口から飛び出した苦しまぎれの冗談____、会議室の空気をむしろ重くした。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits here?

feedback.correct_en: The 「冗談」 is freshly introduced by the long relative clause and functions as the identified cause of what happened. New, specific referents in a single-event report take が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would turn the joke into a contrastive topic (as opposed to something else), which doesn't match the narrator just reporting what the joke did.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の一言が場を凍らせた。
contrast_examples.en: His single remark froze the room. (event report, が)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の一言は、誰も笑わせなかった。
contrast_examples.en: His remark, for its part, made no one laugh. (contrastive は)

prompt.context_jp: 顧客の表情____変わらず、鶸田は額に汗がにじむのを感じた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 顧客の表情____変わらず、鶸田は額に汗がにじむのを感じた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: There's an implicit contrast with Hiwada's reaction in the second clause — the customer's face didn't move, but Hiwada was sweating. Contrastive は naturally pairs the two subjects.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would just report the fact neutrally and lose the pointed contrast the sentence is building between the two people.

contrast_examples.jp: 父は怒らなかったが、母は泣いた。
contrast_examples.en: Father didn't get angry, but mother cried. (contrastive は)
Father got angry. (plain event, が)

prompt.context_jp: 自分が他の人より偉いと思うタイプの上司なら、ここで冷ややかに叱責しただろう。鳩山____そうしなかった。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits given the previous sentence's hypothetical boss?

feedback.correct_en: This line explicitly contrasts Hatoyama with the hypothetical arrogant boss just described. Contrastive は — 'that kind of boss would scold; Hatoyama (by contrast) didn't'.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make it a plain identificational report with no connection to the preceding contrast, flattening the whole point of the paragraph.

contrast_examples.jp: 他の人は怒ったが、彼は笑った。
contrast_examples.en: Others got angry, but he laughed. (contrastive は)
He laughed. (neutral event)

prompt.context_jp: 「鷹野さんの意見を聞かせてよ」投げかけられた質問____、明らかに鷹野に向かって放たれた矢だった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 投げかけられた質問____、明らかに鷹野に向かって放たれた矢だった。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits here?

feedback.correct_en: The question has just been uttered in the previous line — it's now the established topic. The narrator takes it as given and comments on what it really was (an arrow aimed at Takano). This is topic は with an A=B description.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would reintroduce 'the question' as new, which clashes with the fact we just heard it. In 「XはYだった」 identity statements, X is almost always は.

contrast_examples.jp: その言葉は、彼女への警告だった。
contrast_examples.en: Those words were a warning to her. (topic + identity)

contrast_examples.jp: その言葉が彼女を傷つけた。
contrast_examples.en: Those words hurt her. (event, が)

prompt.context_jp: 朱雀に押し出されるようにして、鶸田は営業部____出た。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits with 「出た」 here?

feedback.correct_en: 「〜を出る」 means to exit/leave a place — the departure point is marked with を. Hiwada is leaving the sales department.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「〜に出る」 means to go out to/appear at (e.g. 街に出る), the opposite direction. 「〜で出る」 doesn't fit this verb pattern.

contrast_examples.en: Leave the house.
Appear at the house. (very different)

prompt.context_jp: 鷹野は電卓____取り出し、指先で几帳面にキーを叩き始めた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 鷹野は電卓____取り出し、指先で几帳面にキーを叩き始めた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits with 「取り出し」?

feedback.correct_en: 「取り出す」 is a transitive verb (to take out something), so its direct object — the calculator — takes を.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make the calculator the subject, which clashes with Takano already being the topic doing the action. に doesn't mark objects of 取り出す.

contrast_examples.en: Take out a wallet.
The wallet fell. (intransitive, が)

prompt.context_jp: 気の弱い彼____とって、この沈黙は針の筵に等しい。
prompt.prompt_jp: 気の弱い彼____とって、この沈黙は針の筵に等しい。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle completes the set phrase 「〜とって」?

feedback.correct_en: 「〜にとって」 (for ~ / from the perspective of ~) is a fixed expression. The に marks the person whose viewpoint is being described.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「をとって」 and 「でとって」 are not idiomatic expressions in this sense; learners often confuse this with 「〜について」 but the fixed form here uses に.

contrast_examples.jp: 子どもにとって難しい。
contrast_examples.en: Difficult for a child.
Talk about children. (different pattern)

prompt.context_jp: 隣の鷹野____相変わらず涼しい顔で、まるで自分は無関係だとでもいうように書類を眺めている。
prompt.prompt_jp: 隣の鷹野____相変わらず涼しい顔で、まるで自分は無関係だとでもいうように書類を眺めている。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits here?

feedback.correct_en: Takano is being contrasted with sweating-and-struggling Hiwada from the previous sentences. Contrastive/topic は works perfectly: 'Takano, on the other hand, …'
feedback.incorrect_en: が would simply point out Takano as new info, losing the contrast with Hiwada that drives the whole paragraph.

contrast_examples.jp: 弟は泣いたが、兄は笑っていた。
contrast_examples.en: The younger brother cried, but the older one was laughing. (contrast)
The older brother laughed. (event)

prompt.context_jp: 鶸田はそれを見た瞬間、思わず息____呑んだ。
prompt.prompt_jp: 鶸田はそれを見た瞬間、思わず息____呑んだ。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle completes the set phrase 「息____呑む」?

feedback.correct_en: 「息を呑む」 (to gasp / hold one's breath in surprise) is a fixed idiom with を. The breath is treated as a direct object you 'swallow'.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「息が呑む」 is ungrammatical — 息 cannot be the subject of 呑む. 「息に呑む」 is not a Japanese expression.

contrast_examples.jp: 美しい景色に息を呑んだ。
contrast_examples.en: I gasped at the beautiful scenery.
My breath stopped. (intransitive, different verb)

prompt.context_jp: 鷹野のBGM発言のあと、鶸田は焦っている。
prompt.prompt_jp: このままでは商談が____する。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the word that fits — 'at this rate, the business deal will ___'.

feedback.correct_en: 「空中分解」 (lit. 'break apart in midair') is a common metaphor for a plan or negotiation falling apart before it lands. It fits a sales pitch coming unglued mid-meeting.
feedback.incorrect_en: 空気清浄 means 'air purification' — unrelated. 自由落下 (free fall) exists but isn't the idiom used for negotiations collapsing.

contrast_examples.jp: プロジェクトが空中分解した。
contrast_examples.en: The project fell apart (midway).
A plan gets derailed. (similar meaning, different word)

prompt.context_jp: 気の弱い鶸田にとって、顧客にじっと見つめられる沈黙は耐えがたい。
prompt.prompt_jp: 気の弱い彼にとって、この沈黙は____に等しい。
prompt.prompt_en: Which idiom means 'unbearably uncomfortable to sit through'?

feedback.correct_en: 「針の筵（はりのむしろ）」 — literally 'a mat of needles' — is the set phrase for being in an excruciating, exposed situation, exactly like Hiwada under the customer's silent stare.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「絵に描いた餅」 means 'pie in the sky' (unrealizable plan). 「焼け石に水」 means 'a drop in the bucket' (useless small effort). Neither describes psychological torment.

contrast_examples.jp: 会議中、ずっと針の筵だった。
contrast_examples.en: The whole meeting I was sitting on pins and needles.

contrast_examples.jp: その計画は絵に描いた餅だ。
contrast_examples.en: That plan is pie in the sky.

prompt.context_jp: マミは夫の優しさを認めつつ、くぎを刺す。
prompt.prompt_jp: あなたの そういう優しいとこ ステキだと思うよ。でも、ちょっと____しすぎじゃない？
prompt.prompt_en: Which word fits — the wife is saying he gives his kindness away too cheaply.

feedback.correct_en: 「安売り」 (selling cheap / discounting) is used metaphorically here: he's giving away his kindness too cheaply, letting others take advantage.
feedback.incorrect_en: 値上げ (raising prices) and 買い占め (buying up / hoarding) go the wrong way — the wife's point is that he's undervaluing himself.

contrast_examples.en: Don't sell yourself short.

contrast_examples.jp: 優しさを無料で配っている。
contrast_examples.en: He's giving away his kindness for free. (similar sense)

prompt.context_jp: 鴫石は鳩山に、開発部の負担について語る。
prompt.prompt_jp: あの子たちは、あなたの優しさの____なの。
prompt.prompt_en: Which word fits — Shigeishi says the dev team are ___ of Hatoyama's kindness.

feedback.correct_en: 「犠牲者」 (victim) carries the bite Shigeishi wants: Hatoyama's niceness toward clients ends up hurting the development staff who do the real work.
feedback.incorrect_en: 受益者 (beneficiary) is the opposite of what she means. 後継者 (successor) doesn't fit the context at all.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女は善意の犠牲者だ。
contrast_examples.en: She is a victim of good intentions.
He is a beneficiary of the system.

prompt.context_jp: 鷹野になかなか理解させられないマウス操作を、鳩山はずっと教え続けている。
prompt.prompt_jp: 鳩山は途中で何度もマウス操作の意味を説き直しては、____隣に座り続けた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which adverb best describes how Hatoyama kept sitting next to Takano?

feedback.correct_en: 「根気強く」 (patiently, persistently) captures Hatoyama's defining trait throughout this scene — he keeps teaching without losing his temper.
feedback.incorrect_en: そっけなく (coldly / curtly) is the opposite of his behavior. かろうじて (barely) implies he almost gave up, but the text stresses his steady patience.

contrast_examples.en: Teach patiently.
Answer coldly / curtly.

prompt.context_jp: 鶸田は緊張のあまり、「どこでもドア」の冗談を口にしてしまった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 自分の口から飛び出した____の冗談が、会議室の空気をむしろ重くした。
prompt.prompt_en: Which word describes the kind of joke Hiwada blurted out?

feedback.correct_en: 「苦しまぎれ」 means 'in desperation / as a last resort' — exactly the vibe of a nervous joke pulled out to fill an uncomfortable silence.
feedback.incorrect_en: 念入り (careful, thorough) is the opposite — a prepared joke, not a desperate one. お手盛り (self-serving arrangement) is unrelated.

contrast_examples.en: A desperate excuse.
Prepare carefully.

prompt.context_jp: 顧客が鷹野に「あの提案は君のアイデアだろう」と水を向ける。
prompt.prompt_jp: さあ 何のことでしょう？ 何しろ 私 ＩＴのことは____分からないので。
prompt.prompt_en: Which word fits — Takano is dodging by claiming she understands IT ___.

feedback.correct_en: 「さっぱり分からない」 is the fixed collocation for 'not a clue, completely clueless'. It fits Takano's playing-dumb deflection.
feedback.incorrect_en: ばっちり means 'perfectly / spot on' — the opposite. うっかり (carelessly / by accident) describes a slip-up, not a state of ignorance.

contrast_examples.jp: 意味がさっぱり分からない。
contrast_examples.en: I don't understand a thing.
I memorized it perfectly.

prompt.context_jp: 鶸田は冷や汗。鷹野だけは平然と座っている — この場面で最も自然な言い方は？
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds most natural to describe 'only Takano, calm as ever, is seated in his chair'?

choices.text: 鷹野だけが、涼しい表情のまま椅子に収まっている。
鷹野だけを、涼しい表情のまま椅子に収まっている。
鷹野だけで、涼しい表情のまま椅子に収まっている。

feedback.correct_en: 「〜だけが」 with 収まっている (an intransitive stative) correctly marks Takano as the sole subject. This is the natural pattern for 'only X does/is Y'.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「だけを」 would require a transitive verb taking Takano as object, which 収まる is not. 「だけで」 would mean 'with only Takano', changing the meaning to a means/condition.

contrast_examples.en: Only he remained.
It was solved with just him. (means)

prompt.context_jp: 妻が夫に「人がいいだけじゃなく、便利に使われていないか」と指摘したい場面で、最も自然な表現は？
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds most natural for 'you may not just be nice — you may be someone people take advantage of'?

choices.text: いい人っていうか、都合のいい人になってない？
いい人っていうか、便利な人になってない？
いい人っていうか、使える人になってない？

feedback.correct_en: 「都合のいい人」 is the established idiom for someone others exploit for their own convenience — the exact nuance Mami intends.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「便利な人」 sounds like 'a handy person' (useful in a practical sense), which lacks the negative 'being used' flavor. 「使える人」 is positive — a capable, employable person.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女にとって都合のいい男だった。
contrast_examples.en: He was a convenient (i.e. easily used) man to her.
He is a capable subordinate. (positive)

prompt.context_jp: 物語の第3章の冒頭で、まだ誰も登場していない状態から場面を立ち上げる文。
prompt.prompt_en: Which version is most natural as a scene-opening line introducing the two characters for the first time in the chapter?

choices.text: クライアント先の会議室に、鶸田と鷹野の姿があった。
クライアント先の会議室に、鶸田と鷹野の姿はあった。
クライアント先の会議室で、鶸田と鷹野の姿があった。

feedback.correct_en: A chapter-opening existential uses 〜に〜があった with が for new referents. This is the natural narrative convention.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「姿はあった」 presupposes the figures were already topical and implies contrast ('their figures were there, but...'). 「会議室で」 marks a location of action, not of existence — で/に distinction matters with ある.

contrast_examples.en: There was a cat in the garden. (existence)
A cat was playing in the garden. (action location)
